title: QiT: Quantum-Inspired Transformer for Visual Recognition Task
abstract: Quantum machine learning offers a compelling representational perspective: angle-encoded states inhabit Hilbert spaces in which periodic similarities and interactions can be expressed naturally. Realizing this perspective for visual recognition remains difficult, however, because present quantum neural networks are constrained by limited qubit counts, costly circuit simulation and measurement, noise, and unstable optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. We investigate whether useful structural ideas from quantum models can instead be realized as scalable classical Transformer operations. We introduce QiT, a Quantum-inspired Transformer for vision tasks with three components: (i) angle-inspired encoding that maps image tokens to learned trigonometric Hilbert-space features analogous to quantum rotation-based state encoding; (ii) self-attention over these periodic features, inducing a classical cosine kernel approximated to quantum fidelity kernels; and (iii) gated multiplicative emulation, a trainable classical surrogate for interaction terms found in variational circuits. All components are differentiable tensor operations, so QiT claims neither quantum computation nor quantum speedup and retains the $\mathcal{O}(N^2D)$ attention complexity of a standard Vision Transformer. Across image-classification benchmarks, QiT is competitive with a matched classical Transformer while avoiding the severe runtime cost observed for a small simulated quantum Transformer. QiT-B reaches 78.3\% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 45.7M parameters and 11.5 GFLOPs. These results position QiT as a scalable baseline for isolating and evaluating quantum-motivated inductive biases in visual recognition.
summary: This paper introduces QiT, a Quantum-inspired Transformer that adapts concepts like angle encoding and periodic feature mapping from quantum mechanics into a purely classical, scalable vision model. By doing so, it tests whether quantum-motivated structural biases can improve classical performance without requiring actual quantum hardware. The results show QiT is a competitive and efficient baseline for exploring quantum-inspired inductive biases in computer vision.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of incorporating structural insights from quantum models into scalable classical neural network architectures for visual recognition.
main_result: The proposed model, QiT, achieves competitive performance on ImageNet-1K (78.3% top-1 accuracy) while remaining computationally efficient and avoiding the runtime costs of simulated quantum circuits.
method: QiT integrates three quantum-inspired components into a classical Transformer: angle-inspired encoding, self-attention over periodic features, and a gated multiplicative emulation layer.
model_or_system: QiT is a classical Transformer architecture designed to mimic quantum principles. It uses angle encoding to map image tokens to trigonometric features analogous to quantum rotations, and employs a gated mixer inspired by variational quantum circuits.
key_observables: ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy (78.3%), computational cost (11.5 GFLOPs), and parameter count (45.7M).
important_parameters: The model operates entirely using differentiable tensor operations, maintaining the standard $\mathcal{O}(N^2D)$ attention complexity.
main_assumptions: The model explicitly claims neither quantum computation nor quantum speedup; its performance is evaluated as a classical architecture.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the encoder block using angle encoding and Fourier features; Figure 2 contrasts the explicit cosine feature kernel used by QiT with the circuit-dependent fidelity kernel.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the three classical components (encoding, attention, mixing) motivated by quantum concepts, and validates the architecture's feasibility and performance on standard image classification benchmarks.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is on classical ML, the explicit use of periodic functions and kernel approximations derived from quantum state representations provides a novel, testable inductive bias for deep learning models.

figures.caption: Figure 1. QiT encoder block: Tokens are mapped to a quantum-inspired Hilbert space via angle encoding and Fourier features. Kernel attention approximates quantum fidelity, while local quantum mixers and a circuit surrogate layer emulate bounded-depth PQCs within a Transformer architecture.
Figure 2. Two distinct routes from angle-encoded inputs. QiT uses the explicit cosine feature kernel at the bottom; it does not generally approximate the circuit-dependent fidelity kernel at the top.
Figure 3. Design analogy between a parameterized circuit and the QiT channel mixer. The correspondence motivates the sequence of operations but does not imply equivalent states or functions.
